item.title: Groceries on Installment: The K-Shaped Split Inside America's $18.8 Trillion Debt Pile
item.body:
American household debt has reached a record of roughly **$18.8 trillion**, with about **$1.25 trillion** of that sitting on credit cards. Those are big, round, headline-friendly numbers — and, taken alone, they explain almost nothing.

The more revealing detail is buried underneath. Aggregate balances have largely flattened out. Yet the share of card balances slipping into serious delinquency has stayed stubbornly close to levels the U.S. last saw in the years immediately following the 2008 financial crisis. Those two facts do not fit together comfortably. Debt that is no longer growing quickly should not, in theory, be going bad at a rate reminiscent of a credit downturn.

The explanation is that the national average is now describing two very different populations at once.

---

## The number that stopped moving, and the number that didn't

Quarterly household-debt data compiled by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from a nationally representative sample of consumer credit reports gives the clearest public view of this. It tracks mortgages, auto loans, student loans, and credit cards — and, critically, it tracks *flows*: how much debt moved from current into 30-day, 90-day, and 120-day-plus delinquency each quarter.

Aggregate growth has cooled. Mortgage origination remains constrained by high rates and thin inventory. Card balances, which climbed steeply through the post-pandemic period, have settled into a slower rhythm. On a chart of total balances, the last several quarters look almost calm.

The transition rates do not look calm. The share of credit card balances moving into serious delinquency has hovered near post-2008 highs rather than normalizing back toward the mid-2010s baseline. Auto loans show a related pattern, with subprime borrowers driving most of the deterioration.

When balances flatten but delinquency transitions stay elevated, it usually means the composition of borrowing has shifted. Fewer people are adding debt — but the people still adding it are, on average, less able to service it.

---

## What "K-shaped" actually means here

The letter is a shorthand for divergence: one group's trajectory bending upward while another's bends down, from the same starting point.

**The upper stroke.** Borrowers with prime and super-prime credit scores have been paying down revolving balances. Many locked in mortgages at 3% or lower before 2022 and are effectively insulated from the rate cycle. Their financial assets have appreciated. For this group, higher interest rates have been closer to a feature than a bug — money-market yields and short-duration Treasuries have paid them to hold cash. They are deleveraging by choice, not necessity.

**The lower stroke.** Borrowers in the non-prime tiers are carrying more revolving debt at rates that, for many cards, sit above 20% APR. They are far more likely to rent, which means the housing-cost lock-in that protected homeowners never applied to them. They have absorbed several years of cumulative price increases in groceries, insurance, utilities, and childcare on wages that, for many, rose but not by enough to close the gap.

Average them together and you get "household balance sheets are broadly healthy." That statement is true of the aggregate and misleading about the distribution — which is precisely the problem with reading a $18.8 trillion figure as a single signal.

---

## The part that changes the character of the debt

Here is the shift that matters most, and it is qualitative rather than numerical.

Historically, revolving credit expanded fastest around discretionary consumption — electronics, travel, furniture, holiday spending. Card debt was, broadly, a way to pull forward purchases that could otherwise have waited.

A growing share of new non-prime borrowing now goes toward things that cannot wait. Surveys from the Federal Reserve, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and multiple consumer-finance researchers have documented households using credit cards and short-term installment products for groceries, rent, utility bills, insurance premiums, and medical costs.

Buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) is the clearest illustration. The product was built for mid-ticket discretionary retail — a jacket, a pair of headphones, a mattress. Its fastest-growing use cases increasingly include supermarket orders, food delivery, and everyday essentials split into four payments over six weeks.

Debt used to smooth a shortfall behaves differently from debt used to accelerate a purchase. A television bought on credit is a one-time obligation. Groceries bought on credit recur every week, which means the balance does not naturally retire itself — it compounds against a bill that arrives again in seven days. That is why the delinquency-transition series can stay elevated even as total balances plateau: the borrowing has become less about wants and more about the gap between a paycheck and a fixed monthly cost floor.

---

## The measurement blind spot

There is an important caveat that responsible readings of this data should include: **BNPL is only partially visible.**

Most BNPL "pay-in-four" plans have historically not been furnished to the traditional credit bureaus in the same consistent way as cards and installment loans. Reporting practices have been changing, and major bureaus and lenders have moved toward incorporating this data — but the transition is uneven and recent.

The practical consequence is that the official household-debt total almost certainly understates total consumer obligations, and that a household can appear less leveraged in bureau data than it actually is. It also creates "loan stacking" risk, where a borrower holds several concurrent plans from different providers, none of which can see the others.

This does not invalidate the $18.8 trillion figure. It means the figure should be read as a floor for one category of borrowing, not a ceiling.

---

## Why aggregate stability can persist for a long time

It would be a mistake to read elevated card delinquencies as a forecast of systemic stress. Several structural factors argue against a direct 2008 analogy:

- **Mortgage debt, the dominant component, is qualitatively different this cycle.** Post-crisis underwriting standards, the near-absence of the 2000s-era exotic products, and the enormous stock of fixed-rate loans originated below 4% make the largest slice of household debt unusually resilient.
- **Credit card debt is a small share of the total.** At roughly $1.25 trillion against $18.8 trillion, cards represent under 7% of household liabilities. Severe stress in that segment is painful for the households involved and manageable for the financial system.
- **Lenders have already adjusted.** Card issuers have tightened approval criteria, trimmed credit lines, and provisioned against losses over multiple quarters. The deterioration has not been a surprise to the institutions holding the exposure.

The realistic reading is not "crisis pending." It is that a meaningful and growing minority of households are running a persistent monthly deficit and financing it with the most expensive credit available to them — while the aggregate statistics, dominated by wealthier balance sheets, register that as stability.

---

## What to watch next

For anyone tracking whether the split widens or narrows, a few indicators carry more information than the headline total:

1. **Transition-into-serious-delinquency rates by product**, especially cards and subprime auto — flows lead levels.
2. **Delinquency by credit-score tier and by age cohort.** Borrowers under 40 and those in the lowest score bands have shown the sharpest deterioration.
3. **Revolving credit growth versus real disposable income growth.** When revolving credit outpaces income for consecutive quarters, the gap is being financed rather than closed.
4. **BNPL reporting coverage.** As more of these plans reach the bureaus, expect reported household debt to rise for mechanical reasons. That will be a measurement artifact, not necessarily new borrowing — and it will be widely misread as one.
5. **The composition of what is being financed.** Essentials-driven credit growth and discretionary-driven credit growth carry very different implications for what follows.

---

## The bottom line

A record $18.8 trillion is not, by itself, alarming. Household debt should grow with population, prices, and nominal income; records are the normal state of the series.

What deserves attention is the divergence the total conceals: one group of households retiring debt from a position of strength, another financing groceries at revolving rates because the alternative is going without. Both are inside the same number. Only one of them is captured by the phrase "consumer balance sheets remain solid."

The averages are fine. The distribution is the story.
